question: Is genuine multiclass attack-family classification with truly held-out classes (S2) feasible/defensible for TrustShift's security domain?
source_inspection_staleness_check: src/*.py all last modified 2026-08-15/16, before docs/PHASE3_DESIGN.md was frozen (commit 2294474, 2026-08-22) and before this Phase 3D artifact was written (2026-08-23) -- the inspected code has not changed since the feasibility note was written; the verdict below is not stale.

findings.1_label_definition: src/data.py::label_of() maps every raw label to BENIGN=0 / DDOS=1 / OTHER_ATTACK=-1 -- binary/ternary (attack vs. benign vs. excluded-as-out-of-scope), not a multiclass attack-family task. family_of() computes a family string but is used ONLY for post-hoc, per-family evaluation reporting; the model is never trained to predict family. Identical pattern to TrustShift's own run_pipeline.py (to_binary() + _family() for post-hoc grouping only).
findings.2_class_mapping: src/config.py::FAMILY_PATTERNS/FAMILY_PRECEDENCE uses an explicit longest-match-wins, precedence-tiebreak algorithm; its docstring names the exact bug class TrustShift's own _family() is vulnerable to in principle (a first-match rule would misfile 'DoS slowloris' as volumetric via a bare 'dos' pattern). Checked against TrustShift's actual _family() substring list: no bare 'dos' pattern is present, so 'DoS Hulk'/'DoS GoldenEye'/'DoS slowloris' all resolve correctly -- a near-miss, not a live bug, for the CURRENT label set. TrustShift's algorithm remains less principled in general and should adopt the longest-match+precedence approach before any finer-grained future mechanism work, to avoid relying on having gotten lucky.
findings.3_train_test_split: src/pipeline.py's train_test_split(..., stratify=y) is a plain random row-level split stratified only by binary label -- no capture-file/session grouping. TrustShift's Phase-1 native-file split (validated by the duplicate-rate check in security_provenance_audit.json) is MORE rigorous than this reference project in exactly the respect Phase 1 hardened.
findings.4_held_out_classes_genuinely_absent: Not applicable as asked -- there is no multiclass task to hold classes out of in the reference project either; it never constructs one.
findings.5_multiclass_statistical_meaningfulness: Cannot be assessed from ddos_xdomain_paper (it does not attempt multiclass either). Assessed fresh for TrustShift's own data instead: several families have thin per-family n in their native training files (security_label_space.csv), e.g. netbios=644, portmap=685 rows -- thin for a from-scratch multiclass classifier.

reasoning: The most directly comparable prior work by the same author does not attempt genuine multiclass attack-family classification either, uses the identical binary + post-hoc-family-reporting pattern TrustShift already has, and TrustShift's own per-family sample sizes are thin for several families. Building S2 from scratch to force a distinction the field's own closest precedent avoids would be exactly the kind of manufactured-evidence risk this design gate exists to prevent.
consequence: S1 (binary task, mechanism-coverage severity ladder) is the sole security experiment in Phase 3. Terminology remains locked: S1 measures unseen attack-mechanism / attack-family deployment shift in a binary benign-vs-attack task -- never label-space expansion, never open-set classification, since no class is ever removed from or added to the binary label space.
open_item_not_resolved_here: 3-tier (ddos_xdomain_paper) vs 4-tier (this repo's provenance_audit.py) mechanism-category taxonomy disagreement is documented in PHASE3_DESIGN.md but left for the user to decide before the manuscript describes it -- this does not block S1/S2 execution, only how Phase 4 prose characterizes why mechanisms differ.
